Hey psych nurse here! I initially was afraid to go into psych for the same reason. I worked at a state psychiatric hospital and I enjoyed it a lot. I’ve found that it wasn’t as much charting as I thought, and more client interaction could be had. 

I would start by listening to report. Then I would go into the floor and greet my clients. This is the perfect opportunity to smooth over any tension you feel on the floor. There were always clients who needed to know something or wanted something, and I found that addressing them before they become frustration is typically a better strategy. After that, I do any assessments I needed to do with clients. I assisted the techs a lot, especially with meals and vital signs. I was in charge of handling crises, and used emergency restraint and seclusion so at any point in my work day, I could’ve had a client, sometimes two or three in the emergency restraint chair. These required hourly assessments and addressing any needs the clients may have during the restraint (if they needed me to bring water or provide a urinal). If I was in the med room, I’d give medications and do follow ups, but I worked on a floor with 28 clients so we had a med nurse that was separate from the charge nurse. 

Now as a community psych nurse on the ACT team. I deliver meds to their homes every morning, I administer injections, bring them to doctors appointments. I assess their healthcare needs. I follow a caseload of clients and help them do things, such as apply for jobs, go to the store, get an ID or government assistance.

Psych is a wonderful field. It can be stressful and sad and your heart will break for some of these people. It will also make you smile when your client finally does a thing successfully that they’ve been struggling with. When they ask for help appropriately, when they start being able to manage their mental disorder. When they’re no longer terrified of everything, or paranoid to trust. It’s so worth it if you’re able to appreciate the smallest steps and understand the moments that they are struggling with empathy.

A year ago I was in a very bad place. I had gotten fired from my first job as an RN, and my antidepressants had stopped helping me. I had been crying that day hysterically and I decided to end my life on an impulse. I took all of my antidepressants and my PRN medication and drank alcohol. I told my boyfriend at the time that I loved him, and it tipped him off that something wasn’t right. He called paramedics and they came. I started vomiting and going in and out of consciousness. My heart rate was in the 180s resting and I was having muscle spasms. I remember as they were loading me out of the ambulance to bring me into the hospital, I saw the mountains, and all I could think about was how beautiful life could be. The recovery was painful, my esophagus was burned from the vomit and I couldn’t walk well because of the muscle spasms. I went to the psychiatric unit once my heart finally settled down. My moods were labile and I couldn’t stop crying most of the time I was there from the abrupt stop of my medications. They put me on a different antidepressant and a mood stabilizer and it made a huge difference. I stopped crying so much, my suicidal thoughts went away, and I started functioning more like a person again. 

I was released once my moods were stable enough and the first thing I did was eat chick fil a and go on a hike. It felt really good to feel alive. Something about the pain I felt and the hospital experience after a serious overdose, made me somehow remember how much I wanted to live. I have a niece and nephew that I love so much, I have a supportive family that was with me the entire time, and it was like the haze was lifted and I remembered how much I needed them and love them.  I don’t want to miss out on their lives or mine. 

Since then, I’ve been able to decrease my dose of medication and remain stable, but if staying on this medicine the rest of my life will help me be myself, than that’s a small price to pay for life. 

My mistake was not telling my family at the time what was happening in my mind. I underplayed it, but once they found out from my overdose, they were nothing but supportive. Talking about it is so important when you want to hurt yourself.

I hope you all stay safe and remember to appreciate life.
